title: Do You Know Where Your Holes Are?
author: Craig Latimir
summary: Craig Latimir applies the WWII 'survivorship bias' story -- Abraham Wald's insight that armour should go where the returning planes weren't hit -- to education, arguing that teachers, leaders, and public commentators alike routinely mistake their own successful survival of a system for evidence that the system's supports are unnecessary. He targets critics of explicit teaching methods like phonics, noting that authors who flourished without such methods overlook the far larger group of students who left school with poor literacy under less explicit approaches. He extends the argument to teachers and school leaders who assume, because they personally survived without structured revision instruction or explicit frameworks, that other students and staff don't need them either. His conclusion: successful systems are built for the students who would not otherwise succeed, not just validated by those who did.
points: Latimir's central analogy: WWII engineers nearly reinforced the wrong parts of returning bombers until Abraham Wald pointed out that the planes hit in the 'missing' areas were the ones that never made it back -- a textbook case of survivorship bias.

He argues public criticism of phonics and other explicit teaching methods is frequently survivorship bias in disguise: critics who succeeded without such methods ignore the larger, usually disadvantaged, cohort who didn't.

He cites DfE data that the percentage of Year 1 pupils meeting the expected phonics standard rose from 58% to 82% since the phonics screening check was introduced in 2012, as evidence explicit methods serve students who would otherwise be left behind.

He extends the bias to teachers' and leaders' own assumptions, arguing successful professionals routinely underestimate how much explicit structure less-successful colleagues and students actually need.
quotes: He said that if we only look at the bullet holes of the planes that have survived then we are leaving out a crucial set of data, those that did not.
This is an example of survivorship bias – only looking at the data of those that have 'survived' to inform your decisions.

Since the introduction of the phonics screening check in 2012, the percentage of Year 1 pupils meeting the expected standard in reading has risen from 58% to 82%, with 92% of children achieving this standard by Year 2.
This explicit teaching is not for the few who survived, it is for those who otherwise wouldn’t.

As a teacher, you likely need to give many students more explicit help then you ever received yourself. As a leader, you likely need to give many teachers more explicit help than you ever received yourself.
